--- title: "Day 1 — What is AI engineering?" day: 1 course-section: "01 · Foundations & Setup" est-time: "30 min" status: reviewed objectives: - "Define AI engineering and distinguish it from ML research and data science" - "Map the modern AI stack from hardware up to applications" - "Reason about the build-vs-buy spectrum: prompting, RAG, fine-tuning, pretraining" - "Estimate the token cost of an LLM feature and pick the cheaper model" - "Orient yourself in the 120-day roadmap ahead" prerequisites: - "Basic Python (lists, functions, dictionaries)" notebook: notebooks/01-foundations/01-what-is-ai-engineering.ipynb --- ::: {.tutorial-meta} Day 1 · 01 · Foundations & Setup · ⏱️ ~30 min ::: ::: {.callout-note title="In this tutorial" appearance="simple"} **You'll learn to:** - Define **AI engineering** and place it next to ML research, data science, and software engineering - Read the **modern AI stack** as layers — from GPUs up to user-facing apps - Navigate the **build-vs-buy spectrum**: prompt an API, add retrieval, fine-tune, or pretrain - Put a **dollar figure** on an LLM feature using token economics **Why it matters:** Before you write a single training loop, you need a map. This day gives you the vocabulary and the mental model that every later tutorial slots into — so when we reach LoRA on Day 66 or vLLM on Day 93, you already know *where they live* and *why they exist*. **Prerequisites:** Comfort with basic Python (lists, functions, dictionaries). No ML background assumed. ::: ## What AI engineering is — and isn't **AI engineering is the discipline of building reliable products on top of machine-learning models — especially large pretrained models — and running them in production.** The center of gravity has shifted: a decade ago the hard part was *training* a model from scratch; today a handful of labs train the frontier models and everyone else *adapts and deploys* them. AI engineering is the work in that second clause. It helps to locate the role among its neighbors: | Role | Core question | Typical output | |------|---------------|----------------| | ML researcher | "Can a new architecture learn this better?" | A paper, a novel model | | Data scientist | "What does the data tell us?" | An analysis, a forecast | | ML engineer | "How do I train and serve *this* model at scale?" | A training + serving pipeline | | **AI engineer** | "How do I build a **reliable product** on a pretrained model?" | A shipped feature: RAG, an agent, a fine-tune | The boundaries blur — and you'll touch all four worlds in this course. But the AI engineer's defining constraint is **production**: latency budgets, cost ceilings, evaluation, safety, and the unglamorous reality that a model that's right 95% of the time is wrong one call in twenty. ::: {.callout-tip} A useful litmus test: research optimizes a *metric on a benchmark*; AI engineering optimizes a *product outcome under constraints*. The second almost always involves trade-offs the benchmark never mentions — money, speed, and what happens when the model is confidently wrong. ::: ## The modern AI stack Think of the field as a layered stack. Each layer hides the one below it, and AI engineers mostly live in the top two — but the leaks from lower layers (cost, latency, context limits) are exactly what make the job interesting. ```{mermaid} flowchart TB A["Applications
chatbots · copilots · agents · RAG search"] B["Orchestration
prompts · tools · memory · retrieval · guardrails"] C["Models
Claude · GPT · Llama · embeddings · open weights"] D["Training & adaptation
pretraining · fine-tuning · LoRA · alignment"] E["Serving & infra
vLLM · quantization · KV cache · vector DBs"] F["Hardware
GPUs · TPUs · accelerators"] A --> B --> C --> D --> E --> F ``` You will build something at *every* one of these layers over the next 120 days. A rough map of where the course spends its time: ```{mermaid} flowchart LR S1["Foundations
Days 1–25"] --> S2["Transformers
& internals
Days 26–55"] S2 --> S3["Using LLMs
Days 56–65"] S3 --> S4["Fine-tuning
track
Days 66–95"] S4 --> S5["RAG · Agents
· LLMOps
Days 96–115"] S5 --> S6["Capstone
Days 116–120"] ``` ## The build-vs-buy spectrum When you need a model to do something new, you have a spectrum of options ordered by **cost, effort, and control**. The single most important architectural decision in AI engineering is choosing the *cheapest* point on this spectrum that meets the requirement. ```{mermaid} flowchart LR A["Prompt
an API"] --> B["Add retrieval
(RAG)"] B --> C["Fine-tune
(LoRA / QLoRA)"] C --> D["Pretrain
from scratch"] A -. "more control, more cost, more effort" .-> D ``` - **Prompting** — change behavior with words alone. Minutes to iterate; zero training. Start here. - **RAG** — give the model the *right context* at query time by retrieving from your data. The fix for "the model doesn't know about my documents." - **Fine-tuning** — adjust the model's weights on your examples. The fix for "I need a consistent style/format the prompt can't reliably enforce." (Sections 14–17.) - **Pretraining** — train a base model yourself. Almost never the right answer outside a frontier lab; we build a tiny one on Day 51–55 purely to demystify it. ::: {.callout-tip} Default to the leftmost option that works. Teams routinely reach for fine-tuning when a better prompt or a retrieval step would have solved it in an afternoon for a fraction of the cost. ::: ## Token economics: putting a number on it Most AI features today call a hosted model and **pay per token** — roughly, per word-piece of input and output. Pricing is quoted per *million* tokens, and crucially the **output price is usually several times the input price**. The cost of a single request is: $$ \text{cost} \;=\; \frac{T_\text{in}}{10^6}\, p_\text{in} \;+\; \frac{T_\text{out}}{10^6}\, p_\text{out} $$ where $T_\text{in}, T_\text{out}$ are the input and output token counts and $p_\text{in}, p_\text{out}$ are the per-million-token prices. Multiply by your request volume and this tiny formula drives real architectural choices — caching, model selection, and how much context you dare to stuff into a prompt. ## Worked example Let's estimate the monthly cost of a support-assistant feature. Suppose each request sends ~1,500 input tokens (system prompt + retrieved context + question) and gets back ~400 tokens, and you serve 50,000 requests a month. We'll compare a capable model against a cheaper one. ::: {#635595a4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} def request_cost(t_in, t_out, p_in, p_out): """Cost of one request in dollars. Prices are $ per 1M tokens.""" return (t_in / 1e6) * p_in + (t_out / 1e6) * p_out # Illustrative prices ($ per 1M tokens) — always check current rates. models = { "capable": {"p_in": 3.00, "p_out": 15.00}, "cheap": {"p_in": 0.25, "p_out": 1.25}, } t_in, t_out, volume = 1500, 400, 50_000 for name, price in models.items(): per_call = request_cost(t_in, t_out, price["p_in"], price["p_out"]) monthly = per_call * volume print(f"{name:8s}: ${per_call:.5f}/call → ${monthly:,.0f}/month") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` capable : $0.01050/call → $525/month cheap : $0.00088/call → $44/month ``` ::: ::: Notice how the output tokens dominate despite being fewer in count — that's the higher $p_\text{out}$ at work. The same feature can differ ~10× in cost purely by model choice, before you've changed a line of product logic. *This* is the kind of leverage AI engineering is about. ::: {.callout-tip} A cheap model that's "good enough" on 90% of requests, with the capable model reserved for the hard 10% (a **router**), often beats either model alone on the cost/quality frontier. You'll build patterns like this later in the course. ::: ## Key takeaways - **AI engineering** builds reliable *products* on pretrained models under production constraints — distinct from research (new models) and data science (insight). - The field is a **layered stack**; AI engineers work mostly in applications and orchestration, but lower-layer leaks (cost, latency, context limits) shape every decision. - The **build-vs-buy spectrum** runs prompting → RAG → fine-tuning → pretraining, increasing in cost and control. Default to the cheapest point that works. - **Token economics** turns design choices into dollars; output tokens usually cost the most, and model choice can swing cost by an order of magnitude. ## Check your understanding **1.** In one sentence, what most distinguishes an AI engineer's goal from an ML researcher's? ::: {.callout-tip title="Show answer" collapse="true"} An AI engineer optimizes a **product outcome under production constraints** (cost, latency, reliability, safety), whereas an ML researcher optimizes a **metric on a benchmark**, typically by inventing or improving models. ::: **2.** You need a model to answer questions about your company's internal wiki, which it has never seen. Which point on the build-vs-buy spectrum should you try *first*, and why? ::: {.callout-tip title="Show answer" collapse="true"} **RAG (retrieval-augmented generation).** The problem is missing *knowledge*, not missing *behavior* — so retrieve the relevant wiki passages and put them in the prompt at query time. It's far cheaper and faster to iterate on than fine-tuning, and keeps answers grounded in current documents. ::: **3.** In the cost formula, why can output tokens dominate the bill even when there are fewer of them than input tokens? ::: {.callout-tip title="Show answer" collapse="true"} Because the per-token output price $p_\text{out}$ is typically several times the input price $p_\text{in}$. A small number of output tokens at a high rate can outweigh many input tokens at a low rate — e.g. 400 output tokens at \$15/1M vs 1,500 input tokens at \$3/1M. ::: **4.** Name two "leaks" from lower layers of the stack that an application-layer AI engineer still has to reason about. ::: {.callout-tip title="Show answer" collapse="true"} Any two of: **cost** (token pricing / GPU spend), **latency** (serving and decoding speed), **context-window limits**, and **reliability/failure modes** of the model. These originate in the model/serving/hardware layers but surface directly in the product. ::: **5.** A teammate proposes pretraining a model from scratch to improve answer formatting. What's a cheaper alternative, and what's the general principle? ::: {.callout-tip title="Show answer" collapse="true"} Try **prompting** first (specify the format explicitly), and if that's not reliable enough, **fine-tune** (e.g. LoRA) on formatted examples. The principle: **default to the leftmost / cheapest point on the build-vs-buy spectrum that meets the requirement.** Pretraining is almost never justified outside a frontier lab. ::: ## Coding tasks Work these in the paired notebook — open it in Colab (no GPU needed for Day 1): ### Task 1 — An LLM cost estimator Write a function `monthly_cost(t_in, t_out, volume, p_in, p_out)` that returns the estimated monthly cost in dollars for an LLM feature, where `p_in`/`p_out` are prices per **1 million** tokens and `volume` is requests per month. Then use it to estimate the cost of a feature with 800 input tokens and 250 output tokens at 120,000 requests/month, priced at \$3 / \$15 per 1M tokens. {{< colab notebooks/01-foundations/01-what-is-ai-engineering.ipynb >}} ::: {.callout-tip title="Show solution" collapse="true"} ```python def monthly_cost(t_in, t_out, volume, p_in, p_out): per_call = (t_in / 1e6) * p_in + (t_out / 1e6) * p_out return per_call * volume cost = monthly_cost(800, 250, 120_000, 3.00, 15.00) print(f"${cost:,.2f} / month") # $738.00 / month ``` ::: ### Task 2 — Pick the cheaper model You're given a dictionary of candidate models, each with `p_in` and `p_out` prices per 1M tokens, and a fixed workload (`t_in`, `t_out`, `volume`). Write a function `cheapest(models, t_in, t_out, volume)` that returns the **name** of the model with the lowest monthly cost. Verify it on the dictionary below. {{< colab notebooks/01-foundations/01-what-is-ai-engineering.ipynb >}} ::: {.callout-tip title="Show solution" collapse="true"} ```python def cheapest(models, t_in, t_out, volume): def cost(p): return monthly_cost(t_in, t_out, volume, p["p_in"], p["p_out"]) return min(models, key=lambda name: cost(models[name])) models = { "capable": {"p_in": 3.00, "p_out": 15.00}, "cheap": {"p_in": 0.25, "p_out": 1.25}, "mid": {"p_in": 1.00, "p_out": 5.00}, } cheapest(models, 1500, 400, 50_000) # 'cheap' ``` ::: ## References & further reading - [Anthropic — Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) - [Anthropic — Pricing & models overview](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models) - Chip Huyen, ["Building LLM applications for production"](https://huyenchip.com/2023/04/11/llm-engineering.html) External resources to go deeper than this 30-minute tour allows. Each note says *what* it adds and *why* it's worth your time. - **[*AI Engineering* by Chip Huyen (O'Reilly, 2025)](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/ai-engineering/9781098166298/)** — the definitive book-length treatment of this whole field; an excellent companion to read in parallel with this course. - **[Anthropic's prompt engineering guide](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview)** — concrete techniques for the leftmost (and most underrated) point of the build-vs-buy spectrum; you'll lean on these long before you ever fine-tune. - **[The Illustrated Transformer](https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-transformer/)** — a visual primer on the architecture under every model in the stack; a perfect warm-up for Section 6, where we build self-attention from scratch. - **[Andrej Karpathy — "Intro to LLMs" (1-hour talk)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zjkBMFhNj_g)** — a clear, big-picture mental model of how LLMs are trained and used, from someone who has built them at scale.
